frameworks.name: The Solomon Paradox
frameworks.definition: A decision-making framework using internal dialogue between current self and older self to externalize critique and identify real constraints versus perceived limitations.

frameworks.name: Six M's Constraint Framework
frameworks.definition: A systematic questioning approach (referenced but not fully detailed in transcript) for identifying binding constraints on business growth by iteratively asking why each constraint exists.

claims.text: The founder's calendar is the most malleable resource in a scaling business; a founder who can move from project-driven calendar to capacity-building calendar (recruiting) has the capacity lever to unlock growth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: growth is capped by founder capacity, not market demand
claims.mechanism: Reallocating founder time from direct execution to recruiting A-talent expands company capacity beyond founder's personal capacity ceiling.
bounded_by: Assumes founder is not bottlenecked by market demand or product-market fit
Assumes recruiting can be completed within reasonable timeframe

claims.text: When a founder identifies their single binding constraint (e.g., need for four C-level executives), they should allocate nearly all malleable time to that constraint until it is resolved, rather than distributing effort across multiple priorities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: a clear, singular binding constraint has been identified
the constraint requires time investment (e.g., recruiting, hiring)
claims.mechanism: Concentrating founder effort on the binding constraint removes the bottleneck faster than parallel pursuit of secondary opportunities; once removed, capacity unlock enables all secondary priorities.
bounded_by: Does not apply when multiple constraints are equally binding
Does not apply to market-dependent constraints that cannot be accelerated by founder time

claims.text: Consolidated executive meetings (e.g., marketing, sales, media into one hour) free founder time for bottleneck-focused work; recurring meeting time is the primary lever for reallocation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: recurring meetings exist in founder calendar
founder seeks to reallocate time to constraint-resolution work
claims.mechanism: Eliminating or consolidating low-leverage recurring meetings directly increases the founder's availability for high-leverage activities like recruiting.

anchors.value: 1 hour per week (marketing, sales, media combined)
majority of remaining calendar (100% malleable time)

bounded_by: Assumes meetings can be consolidated without loss of critical coordination
Assumes founder is not required for daily operational execution

claims.text: A-level talent acquisition is the binding growth constraint in scaling service/product businesses; until key executives are hired, secondary opportunities (from the founder's "big list of ideas") should remain unfunded.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business is in growth phase where founder is a bottleneck
founder has identified a roadmap of secondary opportunities
claims.mechanism: Hiring A-level executives expands the company's execution capacity, enabling the founder to delegate operational decision-making and focus on strategic opportunity prioritization.

numbers.axis: company growth stage versus constraint type

anchors.value: founder can evaluate and deploy big-list ideas

bounded_by: Does not apply to hiring routine staff; applies only to A-level executives
Assumes good unit economics make hiring profitable

examples.text: Alex Hormozi's calendar at scale: Mondays feature one consolidated hour covering marketing, sales, and media (previously separate meetings). Outside this single recurring block, his entire week is 100% malleable. Post-product-launch, all reallocation went to recruiting calls, interview preparation, introductions to candidate pipeline, and team betting decisions. This calendar shift persists until he successfully recruits the four C-level executives his business needs to grow beyond founder capacity.

Alex Hormozi uses the Solomon paradox with the "six M's" framework: he internally debates with his older self ("Old Man Mosey") to externalize critique. When facing the question "Why don't you do more?" he responds with constraints ("I can't because of X"), then questions whether those constraints are real ("Why is that limiting you?"). This iterative challenge forces distinction between perceived limitations and true binding constraints, sharpening his decision to allocate all time to recruiting.

practices.text: Use the Solomon paradox—a running internal dialogue with an older version of yourself—to externalize self-critique and separate real constraints from false ones.
Consolidate recurring meetings into minimal blocks; allocate the freed time to addressing the identified binding constraint.
When a single binding constraint is identified (e.g., need for four executives), make recruiting/hiring the sole calendar priority until the constraint is resolved.
